about.tool: A broad-edged pen (the models were laid out with a flat brush) held at about 27° throughout, the angle that tilts the O's stress back and makes the diagonals thick going down to the right and thin going down to the left. Scribes steepen the pen for the thin stems of N and M and flatten it for Z's diagonal; here the angle stays fixed, so those strokes come out heavier (N, M) or lighter (Z) than on the sheet.
about.proportions: Capital height about 9½ nib widths; stems about a tenth of the height. Classical widths: O, Q, C, G, D round, about as wide as high; M and W wide (W's middle strokes cross); H, A, N, K, U, V about as wide as high with their serifs, T, X, Y four fifths; B, E, F, L, P, R, S about half.
about.features: Flat hairline serifs either side of the stems, written as short strokes (the top serif before its stem, the foot serif after); arms end in a short tick. Pointed apexes in A, M, N and V; P's bowl left open; R's leg and Q's very long tail sweep out past the letter. Stems pulled top-down, the round letters in two strokes from the top. Capitals only.
about.history: The inscriptional capitals of imperial Rome (the Trajan column, AD 113, and stones such as Nero's in Cologne, AD 67), painted with a flat brush before they were cut; Edward Johnston's broad-pen study of them is how they are taught today. The Romans had no J, U or W, and no figures but letters: those forms follow the same proportions.
